surfaces.part: asphalt road network on dirt ground (flat terrain tiles, top-down)

answer.evidence: The image is a flat terrain sheet: brown dirt ground with grey-charcoal asphalt road shapes (crossroads, dead ends, 1-wide and 3-wide straight runs). The column scan shows alternating dark charcoal and brown/grey bands that come from the ground texture and the road shapes, not from a standing volume. The roads have a chipped rim and a thin dark ledge on the south edge, only 1-2 rows, which reads as a rim or shadow and not as a vertical front face of 3+ rows. There is no eave, no ellipse and no roof plane. This is a ground autotile drawn top-down, so it has no front face and reads as a flat slab. That is the expected form for terrain.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate's road patches show only about 3 shading steps on the asphalt (dark charcoal body, mid-grey aggregate, a few paler speckles), and the board shows 9 distinct colours in total against 80 for the grass and 7 per tile for the paving. The measured 3 visible tones per tile is well below the paving reference (7) and only equals the grass reference. The 12% near-flat coverage is above the 0% of both references. The edges are tinted (0% neutral dark pixels), and the brown ledge reads as dark material tone, which is fine. But the rim is thin and fairly uniform, with little chipped, broken-face detail. Pale wheel-worn zones are barely visible, so the asphalt reads as one flat grey with sparse speckle. The surrounding soil has fine grain but also only a few tones. Overall it is shallower than the Beodeul references in tone steps and tile density.
